The primary objective of this study is to introduce a novel framework for modeling and analyzing the curvature of deep neural networks (DNNs). We begin by presenting a low-rank approximation of the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix, which is essential for characterizing DNN curvature. Subsequently, we develop a new architecture, the Vision-ViT (ViViT), designed to capture curvature via this low-rank GGN representation. ViViT is constructed by integrating a curvature module into the Vision Transformer (ViT) framework. This module is built upon a low-rank GGN matrix derived from a specific DNN structure. We demonstrate that ViViT can be trained using a straightforward loss function, which is the sum of the squared outputs of the curvature module and the standard ViT loss. Furthermore, we show that ViViT can be trained without any labeled data. Finally, we evaluate ViViT's performance on two tasks: predicting the number of clusters in a dataset and classifying CIFAR-10 images. Experimental results indicate that ViViT achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang1995/ViViT. This study investigates how grammatical gender influences the representations of nouns within gender-marking languages. We begin by analyzing the gender distribution of nouns in German, a language with a balanced gender system, and contrast this with Dutch, which features a highly skewed distribution. Subsequently, we examine the gender characteristics of word embeddings derived from both languages. Our findings indicate that German embeddings capture gender information more effectively than Dutch embeddings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the gender distribution of nouns in a language significantly impacts the gender bias present in its word embeddings. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for gender bias in natural language processing. We demonstrate that the $n$-th homology groups of certain arithmetic groups are generated by a specific class of elements, termed "charms," which are defined via the action of the group on its homology. This class of elements is notably rigid, as it is determined by its behavior in lower degrees. Furthermore, we establish that the "charmability" of these groups is intrinsically linked to their "stiffness," a property that quantifies the extent to which the group's action on its homology is governed by its action on lower-degree homology. We provide explicit calculations of both charmability and stiffness for numerous examples. Additionally, we present a novel proof of the finiteness of the virtual first Betti number for arithmetic groups, which relies on the concept of stiffness. Finally, we outline several open questions and conjectures regarding these properties. We introduce a new task focused on estimating the 3D position of novel category-level objects within a scene, even when no examples of that specific category exist in the training data. This approach is particularly valuable for applications like robot manipulation, where it enables the localization of new object instances without requiring prior exposure to their specific categories. We present a method that leverages a pre-trained object detector to identify novel categories and utilizes a category-agnostic object position estimator to determine their locations. Our results demonstrate that this method can accurately estimate the 3D positions of novel object categories with a mean 3D translation error of 0.22 meters. Furthermore, we show that the method can be extended to estimate the 3D positions of multiple novel object categories within a single scene. Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems, yet it remains difficult due to the complex, non-linear nature of traffic dynamics. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they often fail to generalize well to unseen data. To address this, we introduce a new framework that leverages historical data to identify and extract latent traffic attributes, which are then utilized to enhance prediction accuracy. Specifically, we propose a similarity-based attribute extraction method that identifies attributes by analyzing the similarity between traffic flow and various data sources. Furthermore, we develop a novel deep learning model that integrates these extracted attributes to improve forecasting performance. Extensive experiments on large-scale sparse traffic datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods. Graph autoencoders are widely used to learn latent representations from observed data, yet their utility for answering interventional and counterfactual questions remains unexplored. This paper introduces VACA, a novel variational graph autoencoder designed to address such queries. We introduce a novel dataset comprising 1,000 movies from 2000 to 2019, featuring 11 attributes, including 10 pre-release factors and one post-release metric (gross revenue). Finally, we demonstrate that the predictive power of these attributes differs between domestic and international markets. This study examines the stabilization of voltage dynamics within power grids, focusing on the impact of frequency control mechanisms. We introduce a novel frequency control strategy that leverages the coupling between frequency and voltage to enhance grid stability. Our analysis demonstrates that this alternative control method can stabilize voltage dynamics even when the conventional approach fails. Furthermore, we show that the proposed method can be implemented without altering the existing control infrastructure. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of this new frequency control through numerical simulations. The findings indicate that the proposed control significantly improves grid stability, particularly during severe disturbances. Additionally, the method proves highly effective in mitigating the risks associated with the integration of renewable energy sources. These results underscore the potential of the proposed frequency control to bolster grid stability and facilitate the transition toward a sustainable energy future. We examine the analytic continuation of a real function $f(x)$, defined on a real variable $x$, into the complex plane. We demonstrate that the analytic extension of $f(x)$ can be uniquely determined by its values on a specific subset of the real line, provided this set is sufficiently dense. Furthermore, we establish that the analytic extension of $f(x)$ is uniquely defined by its values on a set of measure zero, as long as this set possesses a Hausdorff dimension exceeding $1/2$. Finally, we illustrate the application of this method to the analytic extension of the Riemann zeta function. Light field (LF) images offer a promising solution for capturing 3D scenes, yet their high data volume and computational complexity hinder practical deployment. This paper introduces a new compression framework that integrates a novel parallax-aware LF image model with a learning-based approach. The proposed parallax-aware model effectively captures the geometric structure of LF images, enabling the compression of a 4D LF image into a compact 3D representation. Additionally, a learning-based method is developed to enhance the compression of this 3D representation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior compression performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the framework is highly efficient, requiring minimal computational resources for both encoding and decoding. Finally, the framework is versatile and can be readily adapted to various LF image acquisition systems. This study investigates the integration of interactive and non-interactive neural architectures within cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) systems. We introduce a straightforward yet effective method for combining these models, which yields substantial performance gains across multiple CLIR benchmarks. Our findings indicate that the optimal fusion strategy varies by dataset, with interactive models excelling in low-resource scenarios and non-interactive models performing better in high-resource contexts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that leveraging multilingual pre-trained language models (PLMs) enhances the efficacy of our fusion approach. Finally, we release a comprehensive evaluation framework for CLIR, comprising 11 datasets and 100+ retrieval models, to facilitate future research in the field. Small-area estimation (SAE) is a statistical approach used to derive reliable estimates for small populations, such as those within specific geographic regions or demographic groups. This technique is vital for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) to generate data for policy decisions and resource allocation. However, SAE models rely on assumptions that may not always hold true in LMIC settings. This study compares design-based and model-based SAE methods using data from the 2017/18 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) in Malawi. The analysis focuses on estimating the prevalence of stunting, underweight, and wasting among children under five, as well as anemia among women of reproductive age. Results indicate that model-based SAE outperforms design-based SAE in terms of precision and accuracy. Furthermore, the study evaluates the impact of including additional covariates and varying the number of clusters in the model. It concludes that model-based SAE is a robust method for LMICs, provided that the model is carefully designed and validated. Finally, the paper offers recommendations for implementing model-based SAE in future surveys. The code used for this analysis is available at https://github.com/abhisheksingh1997/SAE.

The concept of wagering on the measurement outcomes of a quantum state, known as "Kelly Wagering," was introduced in 2014. This paper extends that framework to the continuous-variable domain, where the quantum state is described by a density operator. We demonstrate that the optimal betting strategy involves applying a specific unitary transformation to the state prior to measurement. Furthermore, we establish that the maximum achievable expected payoff is equivalent to the state's purity. Finally, we examine the scenario where the state is unknown, showing that the optimal strategy reduces to a simple projection onto a pure state. This approach yields an expected payoff equal to the fidelity between the unknown state and the chosen pure state. We also provide an explicit construction of the optimal pure state using the eigenbasis of the unknown state's density operator. Additionally, we explore the application of this method to quantum key distribution, specifically the BB84 protocol. In this context, we prove that the optimal strategy for an eavesdropper is to project onto the eigenbasis of the key states, a result that aligns with the well-known optimal attack for BB84. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the security of quantum key distribution. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. The results presented herein were previously published in the proceedings of the 2019 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Communications (ICQC). The study reveals that the band arrangement of these materials is quasiparticle-dependent, with the band gap varying based on the specific element combination. Furthermore, the binding energy of the lowest exciton remains robust against variations in the constituent elements and is unaffected by interlayer stacking configurations. Consequently, these materials exhibit strong potential for applications in optoelectronics and quantum information processing. Finally, the research provides a comprehensive analysis of the quasiparticle band arrangement and excitonic characteristics of MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds. Atmospheric dispersion is a critical factor in high-resolution spectroscopy, necessitating its correction to achieve the highest possible spectral resolution. This correction is typically implemented using an atmospheric dispersion corrector (ADC), which relies on precise knowledge of the atmospheric dispersion function (ADF). However, the ADF is not directly measurable; instead, it must be derived from atmospheric models. This study presents a method for calculating the ADF using on-sky measurements of the atmospheric dispersion introduced by an ADC. We introduce a novel atmospheric model that incorporates the refractive index of air as a function of wavelength, temperature, pressure, and humidity. This model is validated against on-sky data collected at the ESO Very Large Telescope (VLT) using the HARPS-N spectrograph. The results demonstrate that the new model accurately reproduces the measured ADF, with a maximum relative error of 0.001% across the HARPS-N wavelength range. Furthermore, we provide a method to estimate the uncertainty of the ADF based on the uncertainties of the atmospheric model's input parameters. Finally, we compare our findings with existing atmospheric models. The code used to generate these models is publicly available. Consequently, the framework of constant functors and morphisms within compact Hausdorff groups provides a robust foundation for the model theory of compact Hausdorff groups. Specifically, we establish that compact Hausdorff groups are precisely the constant models of a specific first-order theory, and we outline the corresponding constant model companion. Furthermore, we examine the constant theory of compact topological abelian groups, which extends the constant theory of compact Hausdorff groups. Finally, we present several illustrative examples of constant models for this latter theory. The primary technical instrument employed throughout this work is the concept of a locally compact group equipped with a distinguished compact subgroup. This notion is introduced and analyzed in detail, as it plays a crucial role in our methodology. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the constant model theory of locally compact groups, a subject that has not previously been addressed in the literature. This discussion is particularly significant because it elucidates the relationship between the constant model theory of compact Hausdorff groups and the classical model theory of compact Hausdorff groups. We also explore the constant model theory of totally disconnected locally compact groups, which extends the constant theory of compact Hausdorff groups. In this context, we demonstrate that the constant theory of totally disconnected locally compact groups is the model companion of the constant theory of compact totally disconnected groups. Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning framework designed to train models on decentralized data while safeguarding user privacy. This paper examines the challenges of fairness and privacy within FL, specifically focusing on differential privacy (DP). We first analyze the impact of DP noise on fairness, demonstrating that it can exacerbate bias in federated models. Subsequently, we introduce a novel approach to achieve fairness-privacy trade-offs in FL by leveraging the concept of fairness-privacy sensitivity. We establish a lower bound for this sensitivity and propose a new algorithm that utilizes it to balance fairness and privacy. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our method through extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The results indicate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of fairness-privacy trade-offs. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/FL-FairDP.

This study introduces a new framework for an IRS-assisted wireless powered network that accounts for interference. The system comprises a power station, a single-antenna user, an IRS, and an interferer. The power station transmits energy to the user, while the IRS reflects this energy to enhance the user's received power. Simultaneously, the interferer transmits information to the user, creating interference that degrades the user's throughput. To mitigate this, the user employs a power allocation strategy to maximize throughput, while the IRS optimizes its phase shift to further improve performance. The resulting optimization problem is non-convex and difficult to solve. To address this, we propose a deep unsupervised learning approach that eliminates the need for channel state information (CSI) at the power station. This method enables the power station to determine the optimal power allocation strategy and the IRS to calculate the optimal phase shift without requiring CSI. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, the approach exhibits robustness against channel estimation errors and remains effective even when the power station possesses imperfect CSI. Finally, we analyze the computational complexity of the proposed method. The results indicate that the approach is computationally efficient, making it suitable for practical implementation. In summary, the proposed deep unsupervised learning approach offers a promising solution for enhancing the throughput of IRS-assisted wireless powered networks in the presence of interference. This work provides valuable insights for the design and deployment of such networks. Additionally, the approach can be extended to other scenarios, including multi-user and multi-antenna systems. Overall, this research contributes to the advancement of wireless communication systems by offering a novel and effective method for throughput enhancement in IRS-assisted wireless powered networks. The proposed approach is expected to have significant practical applications in future wireless communication systems. Furthermore, the deep unsupervised learning technique employed can be utilized in various other wireless communication scenarios, such as cognitive radio networks and device-to-device communication. In conclusion, this work presents a valuable contribution to the field of wireless communication, offering a new perspective on throughput enhancement in IRS-assisted wireless powered networks. The proposed approach is anticipated to inspire further research and development in this area. We establish the Ward identities for the primary fields within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. These identities are expressed using the three-point correlation functions of the theory. As a practical application, we utilize these relations to compute the four-point correlation functions of primary fields. Our findings align with those previously reported in the literature. This work serves as a foundational step toward investigating the integrable system linked to the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. Consequently, this result provides a novel method for constructing classical solutions to the integrable system. We anticipate that these results will be valuable for future research. Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) offers a significant advantage over conventional quantum key distribution by tolerating higher channel loss, a benefit that becomes even more pronounced in the twin-field variant. This advantage stems from the twin-field protocol's reliance on phase locking only at the central node, rather than at every node. However, this requirement has previously hindered the development of twin-field quantum key exchange (TF-QKE) over existing fiber networks. In this work, we demonstrate that TF-QKE is feasible without phase locking at the central node by employing a novel phase estimation technique. We validate this approach through a 100-km fiber experiment, successfully generating a secret key. Furthermore, we show that this method can be extended to multi-user TF-QKE, enabling the sharing of a secret key among multiple users. Our findings pave the way for the practical implementation of twin-field quantum key exchange over current fiber infrastructure. We provide explicit descriptions of the Toeplitz algebras associated with the Fock and Hardy spaces for the circle group. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Toeplitz algebra for the Fock space is isomorphic to the tensor product of the Toeplitz algebra for the Hardy space and the algebra of compact operators. Furthermore, we establish that the Toeplitz algebra for the Fock space possesses a simple structure. Additionally, we confirm that the Toeplitz algebra for the Hardy space is isomorphic to the C*-algebra of continuous functions from the circle to the Calkin algebra. Finally, we prove that the Toeplitz algebra for the Hardy space is not nuclear. These findings are derived using a novel approach that relies on the representation of the circle group on the Fock space. This method is also applicable to Toeplitz algebras defined on the Fock space of a compact Lie group. Finally, we outline several open questions regarding these algebras. We present a new analysis of the gas distribution surrounding the S1 cluster in the Rho Ophiuchus dark cloud, utilizing data from the Herschel Gould Belt survey. By examining the spatial relationship between the S1 cluster and the gas, we identify a distinct cavity in the molecular gas, which we attribute to the combined effects of stellar feedback and the cloud's internal dynamics. We also investigate the distribution of ionized gas, atomic hydrogen, and photodissociation regions (PDRs) within the cloud. Our findings indicate that the PDRs are primarily shaped by the S1 cluster, with a notable exception in the southern region where a PDR is illuminated by the nearby S10 cluster. Furthermore, we observe a correlation between the ionized gas and the PDRs, suggesting that the ionized gas is confined to the PDRs. While deep learning has significantly advanced research in this domain, the Transformer architecture has become the dominant model for various natural language processing tasks. This survey examines the application of Transformers to veracity-related challenges, offering a comprehensive overview of the field. This study investigates the impact of time-varying versus time-invariant factor loadings on mortality prediction. We introduce a time-varying factor model for mortality rates and develop a novel estimation approach utilizing a time-varying factor analysis framework. Our findings indicate that time-varying factor loadings enhance the accuracy of mortality rate forecasts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that time-varying factor loadings are essential for predicting mortality rates, whereas time-invariant factor loadings are more effective for forecasting life expectancy. Finally, we apply these models to predict mortality rates and life expectancy for the United States. The results show that the time-varying factor model outperforms the time-invariant factor model in predicting mortality rates, while both models perform similarly regarding life expectancy predictions. Additionally, the time-varying factor model surpasses the Lee-Carter model in predicting mortality rates, though it yields comparable results for life expectancy. Overall, the time-varying factor model proves superior for mortality rate prediction, while the time-invariant factor model is preferable for life expectancy prediction. These insights can inform the selection of appropriate models for mortality prediction. This study introduces a Bayesian approach for evaluating translator reliability. We model the translation process as a two-stage mechanism: first, a translator generates a noisy version of the source text, and second, a post-editor refines it to match the target. We assume that both the translator and the post-editor introduce errors independently. By analyzing a collection of source, translated, and post-edited texts, we can estimate the error rates for both parties. Our method relies on a straightforward probabilistic model and employs a straightforward Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm to derive posterior distributions for the error rates. We validate this approach using both simulated data and a real-world dataset. The results demonstrate that our method effectively estimates error rates for both translators and post-editors. Furthermore, we show that the method can be extended to estimate error rates for multiple translators working on the same source text. Finally, we illustrate how these error rate estimates can be utilized to assess the quality of machine translation post-editing. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/roberts1999/Translator-Reliability.

We introduce a sum rule for energy deposition in scattering systems, expressed as a weighted integral of the energy deposition eigenchannel spectrum. This rule is derived from the conservation of energy and momentum, the conservation of particle number, and the detailed balance condition. We demonstrate its application to two-dimensional electron scattering off a single impurity and electron-phonon scattering. Additionally, we propose a method to calculate the energy deposition spectrum in a two-dimensional electron gas under a magnetic field, which could be validated through experiments involving inelastic electron tunneling spectroscopy. Finally, we outline a potential experimental setup to observe this sum rule in a two-dimensional electron gas. These findings are particularly relevant for investigating energy dissipation in quantum Hall edge states and the associated non-equilibrium phenomena. Furthermore, our results may have broader implications for other scattering processes, such as phonon-phonon interactions. The sum rule is also applicable to systems with broken time-reversal symmetry, including those with a magnetic field, spin-orbit coupling, or superconductivity. In these cases, the detailed balance condition is modified by the presence of a chemical potential, which can be non-zero due to the system's non-equilibrium state. This modified condition is essential for deriving the sum rule in such scenarios. We also discuss the implications of our findings for the study of non-equilibrium phenomena in quantum systems. Our results suggest that the energy deposition spectrum can be used to probe the system's relaxation processes and to test the validity of the detailed balance condition. We introduce a novel approach to lottery ticket valuation that incorporates the buyer's anticipated future behavior. Our findings indicate that ticket prices are contingent upon the buyer's expected future spending, leading to a dynamic pricing model where costs fluctuate over time. Furthermore, we propose a strategy for sellers to optimize their revenue by selling tickets at specific intervals. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this dynamic pricing mechanism can significantly enhance seller profits. Additionally, we examine the impact of price fluctuations on the seller's expected number of sales. Finally, we outline the model's limitations and suggest potential avenues for future research. The valley degree of freedom in two-dimensional materials is a promising candidate for next-generation electronic and spintronic devices. However, electron-phonon coupling can significantly impact valley physics, yet its influence remains poorly understood. This study investigates how various electron-phonon coupling mechanisms affect valley physics in two-dimensional materials. We demonstrate that the deformation potential mechanism is the primary driver of electron-phonon scattering, while the piezoelectric mechanism plays a secondary role. Furthermore, we show that the spin-orbit coupling mechanism can induce intervalley scattering, thereby reducing valley polarization. Finally, we establish that the spin-valley coupling mechanism is the sole source of spin relaxation within the valley degree of freedom. These findings offer valuable insights for the design of valleytronic devices. Additionally, we provide a Python package, named "valleyphonon," to facilitate the calculation of electron-phonon scattering rates and spin relaxation times in two-dimensional materials. t-SNE is a widely used dimensionality reduction technique that has become a standard tool for visualizing high-dimensional data. However, it relies on Euclidean distance, which is unsuitable for data residing on a sphere. This paper introduces a novel approach for spherical data by integrating t-SNE with the geodesic distance metric. We demonstrate that this new method, termed spherical t-SNE (s-t-SNE), is mathematically equivalent to t-SNE when using the geodesic distance between two points on a sphere. Experimental results indicate that s-t-SNE produces superior visualizations compared to Euclidean t-SNE, particularly for data with constant curvature. Additionally, we show that s-t-SNE can be efficiently computed using the Fast Marching Method. Finally, we apply s-t-SNE to visualize the 3D shapes of proteins. Specifically, for any graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, the value of the polynomial evaluated at $x=1$ corresponds to the count of independent sets in $G$. We demonstrate that the coefficients of these polynomials adhere to a log-concavity property. Furthermore, we establish that the roots of $\mathcal{P}_n$ are real and negative, and we derive an upper bound for their absolute values. Additionally, we present a lower bound for the second-largest root of $\mathcal{P}_n$. Finally, we provide an asymptotic analysis of the polynomials $\mathcal{P}_n$ as $n$ approaches infinity. This study investigates how remote work impacts the success of Scrum projects. By integrating a systematic literature review with a survey of 100 Scrum practitioners, we identified key factors influencing remote Scrum success. Our findings indicate that remote work significantly affects the Scrum process, particularly regarding communication, collaboration, and team dynamics. Furthermore, we observed that remote environments tend to diminish the influence of the Scrum Master and Product Owner, while increasing the responsibilities of the Development Team. These insights are supported by a comprehensive analysis of the collected data. Ultimately, this research offers valuable guidance for organizations aiming to implement Scrum in remote settings. This paper presents formulas for the Gau-Wu value of $4\times 4$ matrices and specific arrowhead matrices. The Gau-Wu value is a real-valued function defined on square matrices that serves as a generalization of the determinant. It is particularly valuable in the numerical solution of partial differential equations, as it enables the construction of a class of positive definite matrices. Additionally, the Gau-Wu value is closely linked to the Gauss-Seidel method for solving linear systems. The study begins by deriving the value for $2\times 2$ matrices, followed by the derivation of formulas for $4\times 4$ matrices and selected arrowhead matrices. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the results. The primary objective is to provide explicit formulas for the Gau-Wu value of $4\times 4$ matrices, which can be applied to larger matrices by partitioning them into $4\times 4$ blocks. Furthermore, the study aims to derive explicit formulas for arrowhead matrices, which are frequently encountered in the numerical resolution of partial differential equations. The paper also includes illustrative examples to demonstrate the application of these formulas. Ultimately, this work seeks to facilitate the calculation of the Gau-Wu value for $4\times 4$ matrices and specific arrowhead matrices, thereby supporting the numerical solution of partial differential equations. The findings are expected to be useful for researchers and practitioners in the field of numerical analysis. Furthermore, the $p_{\rm T}$ dependence of the $v_2$ for electrons from charm-hadron decays exhibits a similar trend to that of electrons from light hadron decays. This suggests that the $v_2$ of electrons from charm-hadron decays is primarily driven by the collective flow of the medium, with only a minor contribution from the $v_2$ of the charm quarks themselves. Additionally, the $v_2$ of electrons from charm-hadron decays shows a stronger dependence on $p_{\rm T}$ compared to electrons from light hadron decays, a characteristic also seen in the $v_2$ of D mesons. This study introduces a novel method for analyzing the chromaticity of images by employing persistent homology. We begin by defining a new class of image representations termed "chromatic alpha structures," which are derived from a specific class of functions known as "alpha shapes." These structures are constructed by segmenting an image into chromatic regions and assigning each region a value corresponding to its chromaticity. We then demonstrate how to generate a chromatic alpha structure from any given image. Finally, we apply persistent homology to these chromatic alpha structures to extract features that characterize the image's chromaticity. Experimental results indicate that these features effectively capture the chromaticity of both natural and synthetic images. Furthermore, we show that these features can be utilized to distinguish between natural and synthetic images, as well as to differentiate between images with varying chromaticity. Formal concept analysis (FCA) is a mathematical framework used to categorize data based on shared attributes. However, when applied to large datasets, FCA often generates an excessive number of concepts, rendering the resulting categorization difficult to interpret. This paper introduces a method to adapt FCA by integrating Dempster-Shafer theory, which enables the combination of evidence from multiple sources. This approach allows for the aggregation of concepts into higher-level categories, thereby enhancing the comprehensibility of the categorization process. The proposed method is demonstrated through an application to the auditing domain. Additionally, the paper outlines a strategy for selecting the most appropriate concepts for aggregation, ensuring that the final categorization remains both interpretable and faithful to the original data. Finally, the study includes a case study to illustrate the method's application. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robinvanbesien/adaptable-fca.

The stitching technique, which involves combining two point processes to generate a new one, has been utilized to create novel point processes. This paper extends the stitching method to the Strauss process by applying it to two independent Strauss processes. We derive the parameters of the resulting process and demonstrate that it remains a Strauss process. Furthermore, we establish the conditions under which the new process exhibits complete spatial randomness. Finally, we provide an algorithm for simulating this stitched process. The study includes several examples to illustrate the method, and a simulation study is conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm. Additionally, we apply the stitching technique to the log-gas point process, showing that the resulting process is a Strauss process. We derive the parameters of this new process and determine the conditions for complete spatial randomness. An algorithm for simulating this log-gas point process is also provided. The paper concludes with examples and a simulation study to assess the performance of the algorithm. The source code is available at https://github.com/AnushaKumar2000/Creating-from-the-Strauss-Process-using-stitching. The generalized uncertainty principle (GUP) is a widely accepted framework in quantum gravity that extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. This study examines the effects of the GUP on both Galilean and Lorentz transformations. Under the GUP, the commutation relation between position and momentum is modified, leading to a revised uncertainty relation. Consequently, the standard transformation laws for position and velocity are altered. The paper derives the modified Galilean and Lorentz transformations and analyzes their implications. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the GUP introduces a fundamental limit to the precision of position measurements. Finally, the study explores the impact of the GUP on the energy-momentum relation. The results indicate that the GUP imposes an upper bound on momentum, whereas no such limit exists for energy. Additionally, the GUP causes the group velocity to exceed the speed of light, a phenomenon that does not violate relativity because the phase velocity remains below this limit. Finally, the GUP is shown to induce a redshift in the energy-momentum relation. These findings suggest that the GUP may have observable consequences in high-energy physics. This model is applicable to various scenarios, including distributed computing, parallel processing, and multitasking systems. We demonstrate that the proposed allocation problem is NP-hard and provide an approximation algorithm with a performance guarantee. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the approximation ratio and show that our algorithm achieves this bound. The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, with billions of devices anticipated by 2025. These devices are increasingly deployed in critical sectors like healthcare, transportation, and smart cities, where dependability is paramount. However, the inherent resource limitations of IoT hardware make it difficult to implement robust security measures, such as firmware updates, which are essential for protecting against cyber threats. This paper introduces a dependable firmware update mechanism for IoT devices, specifically targeting large-scale mesh networks. We conducted a comprehensive performance evaluation of this mechanism across various network sizes and topologies, including both indoor and outdoor environments. Our results demonstrate that the proposed approach is highly scalable, capable of supporting up to 1000 devices with a maximum update time of 10 minutes. Furthermore, the mechanism ensures that no more than 10% of devices are offline during the update process. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the mechanism's performance and discuss its potential applications. The source code is available at https://github.com/rajkumar1999/DependableIoTUpdates. We investigate the multifractal characteristics of the Fock-space wave function within the one-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg model, focusing on the transition from many-body localized to delocalized phases. By analyzing the scaling of the Fock-space propagator, we identify a critical point that aligns with the many-body localization transition. Furthermore, we observe that the multifractal spectrum exhibits a shift in the delocalized phase, a phenomenon we attribute to the presence of a spinon. These findings are corroborated by numerical simulations. Our results indicate that the Fock-space propagator serves as a robust indicator for detecting the many-body localization transition. Additionally, we demonstrate that the multifractal spectrum can be utilized to distinguish between localized and delocalized phases. Finally, we establish that the multifractal spectrum in the delocalized phase adheres to the scaling laws predicted by conformal field theory. These insights offer a deeper understanding of the many-body localization transition and the associated critical phenomena. This study addresses a search problem where a searcher must locate $k$ targets within a large, unknown environment. The searcher can query a limited number of locations, receiving binary feedback indicating whether each queried spot contains a target. The objective is to minimize the total number of queries required to find all $k$ targets. We introduce a new algorithm that achieves a constant-factor approximation for this problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach is nearly optimal by proving that no algorithm can achieve a better approximation ratio. Finally, we validate the practicality of our method through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/BILIS.

Machine learning models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where minor, imperceptible perturbations to input data can cause significant classification errors. This study investigates the creation of such perturbations for quantum classifiers, specifically the variational quantum classifier (VQC). We demonstrate that adversarial instances can be generated by applying a quantum circuit to the input state, which is subsequently fed into the VQC. Furthermore, we show that these adversarial inputs can be produced using a single, universal quantum circuit. Finally, we explore the potential of these generated adversarial instances for enhancing the robustness of quantum classifiers. Our findings indicate that adversarial training is feasible with these instances, resulting in a VQC that is more resilient to adversarial attacks. Additionally, we observe that the resulting quantum classifier exhibits greater robustness against noise compared to its classical counterpart. These results suggest that adversarial training is a promising strategy for developing robust quantum machine learning models. Conformance checking is a core component of process mining, where it is common for logs to contain partial traces that do not fully align with the process model. This paper introduces a method for verifying the conformance of such partial traces against a process model represented as a Petri net. The approach relies on infix alignments, which are specifically designed to handle partial traces. To enhance efficiency, the method is extended to utilize postfix alignments, which are optimized for partial traces that extend beyond the model's scope. The proposed technique is evaluated through a case study and compared against existing methods. The results demonstrate that the approach is both effective and efficient, particularly when dealing with partial traces that exceed the boundaries of the process model. Furthermore, the method is applicable to any process model that can be translated into a Petri net. The implementation is available as an open-source tool. The paper also addresses several limitations and outlines potential future research directions. Finally, the study includes a tutorial on using the tool to verify the conformance of partial traces. Radio transmission modeling is essential for analyzing and designing cellular networks. While traditional methods rely on empirical models, ray-tracing, or stochastic geometry, this paper introduces a novel approach using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). This method is trained on a dataset generated by a ray-tracing simulator, which accounts for the physical environment and the specific characteristics of the radio signal. The proposed model demonstrates high accuracy in predicting received signal strength and is computationally efficient enough for real-time applications. Furthermore, it can be deployed on mobile devices to enable radio signal analysis for applications such as network planning and optimization. The model's performance is validated through extensive simulations and a real-world case study. Results indicate that the model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.1 dB and a correlation coefficient of 0.999 when compared against a ray-tracing simulator. Additionally, the model is capable of predicting received signal strength for various radio signals, including 5G NR, LTE, and Wi-Fi. Finally, the paper provides a detailed analysis of the model's computational complexity and memory requirements. The source code is available at https://github.com/robin-lee/DeepRadio. Power system expansion models are extensively utilized to forecast future electricity generation and consumption, yet their outputs are highly sensitive to input parameters. This study examines how variations in input data influence model results, specifically focusing on the responsiveness of power system expansion models. We analyze the impact of input changes on output variability and the resulting uncertainty in future electricity production. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this uncertainty for policy-making and the design of future power systems. Our findings indicate that while model outputs are highly responsive to input changes, this sensitivity is not uniform across all parameters. Consequently, we recommend that future research prioritize the uncertainty of those input parameters that exert the greatest influence on model outcomes. Additionally, we propose that the uncertainty inherent in model outputs should be explicitly incorporated into policy decisions. Finally, we suggest that the responsiveness of these models warrants further investigation to enhance the reliability of policy guidance derived from them. This paper establishes the global well-posedness of the Vlasov-Poisson-like system within a bounded domain. The system consists of a kinetic equation for the distribution function and a boundary value problem for the electric potential, featuring a specular reflection boundary condition for the distribution function and a Neumann boundary condition for the potential. The analysis demonstrates that the distribution function remains non-negative and bounded globally in time, while the electric potential is shown to be bounded globally in time as well. Furthermore, the study proves the existence of a global attractor for the system. These findings extend previous results, which were limited to the whole space or periodic settings. Additionally, the methodology employed is applicable to other Vlasov-Poisson-like systems, such as those involving the Vlasov-Maxwell system or the Vlasov-Boltzmann-Poisson system. Finally, the paper includes an appendix detailing the proof of the existence of a global attractor. The primary innovation of this work lies in the development of a novel technique for deriving a priori estimates of the electric potential. This approach relies on a specific identity for the distribution function, which is derived from the kinetic equation and boundary conditions, and on a specific identity for the electric potential, which is derived from the potential equation and boundary conditions. This technique is expected to be valuable for future research on Vlasov-Poisson-like systems. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the Vlasov-Poisson-like system and its associated boundary conditions; Section 3 presents the main results; Section 4 provides the proofs of these results; and Section 5 contains the appendix. Concept location involves identifying the source code files and lines that implement a specific concept within a software system. This paper introduces STRICT, a novel approach that leverages information retrieval to pinpoint concepts. STRICT constructs a system-wide index of concepts and their associated code snippets, then retrieves the most relevant snippets for a given concept using a learned ranking model. To identify the concept's location, STRICT analyzes the search keywords embedded in these retrieved snippets. STRICT was evaluated on 100 open-source Java projects, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness. The source code for STRICT is accessible at https://github.com/rohitkumar1999/STRICT. The authors plan to release the concept location dataset used in this study. Additionally, the authors intend to explore the application of STRICT for other software maintenance tasks. The stable matching problem involves pairing two groups of agents based on their mutual preferences. While the Gale-Shapley algorithm is a well-known solution, it is not the only approach. This paper introduces a new algorithm that allows agents to strategically choose which proposals to submit. We demonstrate that this method is strategy-proof, meaning agents have no incentive to deviate from truthful reporting. Furthermore, we establish that the algorithm runs in polynomial time and prove that the resulting stable matchings are Pareto optimal. Finally, we provide an example to illustrate the algorithm's mechanics. The source code is available at https://github.com/robinson1998/Matching. Although automatic evaluation metrics for summarization have advanced significantly, they still struggle to accurately reflect human judgments. This paper introduces SummScore, a comprehensive metric designed to assess summary quality by leveraging a cross-encoder. SummScore evaluates summaries across three dimensions: fluency, relevance, and coherence. To address the challenge of data scarcity for fluency and coherence, we utilize a pre-trained language model to generate pseudo-references, which are then used to train a BERT-based classifier. For relevance, we employ a BERT-based classifier trained on a dataset of human-annotated summary-passage pairs. Extensive experiments on the CNN/DailyMail and XSum datasets demonstrate that SummScore achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.60 with human scores, outperforming existing metrics. This study introduces a novel algorithm designed to reconstruct a signal from quadratic measurements. The method employs a gradient descent approach, utilizing a specific step size to ensure convergence toward the signal's $\ell_2$-norm. We demonstrate that this step size guarantees convergence to the signal's $\ell_2$-norm even when the number of measurements is below the signal's sparsity level. Furthermore, we establish that the algorithm converges to the signal's $\ell_1$-norm under the condition that the number of measurements exceeds the signal's sparsity. Finally, we present numerical results to validate the algorithm's performance. These findings indicate that the method is highly effective for signal recovery, particularly when the measurement count is less than the signal's sparsity. Additionally, the algorithm demonstrates robustness against noise and maintains a low computational cost. The proposed approach is applicable to signal recovery scenarios involving quadratic measurements, such as phase retrieval and compressive sensing. We present a comprehensive numerical analysis of the thermal profile generated within a liquid by a laser beam. This profile is derived by solving the heat diffusion equation, which incorporates a heat source term dependent on the laser's intensity and the liquid's absorption coefficient. The resulting thermal profile is subsequently utilized to calculate the self-induced diffraction pattern of the beam. Our findings indicate that the complex structures observed in the diffraction pattern are directly linked to the intricate features of the thermal profile. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the thermal profile can be effectively modeled using a superposition of two Gaussian functions. This approach offers a straightforward method for predicting the diffraction pattern based on the laser's absorption coefficient and power. Finally, we show that the thermal profile can be accurately described by a single Gaussian function when the absorption coefficient is sufficiently high. These results are validated through numerical simulations of the diffraction pattern. Our study provides a thorough numerical characterization of the thermal profile in a liquid, thereby enabling a deeper understanding of the complex self-induced diffraction patterns. Additionally, we establish a clear relationship between the thermal profile and the diffraction pattern, which can be effectively approximated using a superposition of two Gaussian functions. This work holds significant potential for applications in laser machining and the study of laser-induced phase transitions. The proposed methodology is also applicable to other scenarios involving laser-induced thermal profiles in liquids. Ultimately, our findings offer a robust framework for predicting the thermal profile and the resulting self-induced diffraction pattern. This framework can be extended to various applications, including laser machining and the investigation of laser-induced phase transitions. This paper introduces a new framework for validating neural networks (NNs) within control systems. We propose a method to calculate the worst-case error of an NN controller relative to a reference controller, which is essential for safety-critical applications. The approach involves training the NN to minimize the error against the reference controller across a specific state space, followed by a validation step that determines the region where the NN's error remains within a predefined threshold. This validation process is formulated as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) and solved using off-the-shelf optimization software. The method is demonstrated on a quadrotor case study, where an NN controller is trained to match a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) controller, and the resulting validation region is computed. Furthermore, we extend this approach to handle continuous-time systems by employing a discrete-time approximation. Finally, we evaluate the method's scalability by testing it on a 10-dimensional system. The proposed validation technique is applicable to any reference controller, including those based on neural networks. Additionally, the method can be adapted to validate NN observers and filters by assessing the worst-case error between the NN and a reference observer/filter. Our findings indicate that the energy spectrum remains independent of the dissipation rate, provided the rate is sufficiently low. Furthermore, we observe that the energy spectrum is insensitive to the specific form of the dissipative sink, as long as the sink's action is localized at high wavenumbers. These results are corroborated by numerical simulations of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation incorporating a dissipative term. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the energy spectrum of a system governed by the wave equation with a dissipative term. This power-law spectrum persists at high wavenumbers, contingent upon the dissipative term being localized at sufficiently high wavenumbers. This paper introduces a novel iterative graph normalization technique designed to identify maximum weight independent sets. The approach is grounded in the observation that the weight of a maximum weight independent set in a graph $G$ equals the minimum weight of a vertex cover in $G$. The study examines the properties of this normalization process and demonstrates its application to both weighted and unweighted graphs. Furthermore, the authors establish a sufficient condition for the existence of a maximum weight independent set within the normalized graph. Finally, the paper presents several illustrative examples to clarify the method. The authors hope this work will inspire further research into graph normalization and the determination of maximum weight independent sets. Additionally, they intend to extend this study to other graph optimization problems, such as minimum dominating sets and maximum clique problems. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides the necessary definitions and notations; Section 3 outlines the iterative graph normalization method; Section 4 analyzes the properties of this method; Section 5 applies the method to weighted graphs; Section 6 addresses unweighted graphs; Section 7 offers examples; and Section 8 concludes the study. We report the detection of low-frequency radio emission from the flare star binary system CR Draconis, observed using the LOFAR radio telescope. This emission is identified as electron-cyclotron maser radiation, characterized by a narrow bandwidth of approximately 100 kHz and a duration of roughly 10 minutes. The source's position aligns with the known location of the binary, and the observed flux density of 0.1 mJy at 140 MHz indicates a brightness temperature exceeding 10^15 K. The emission's periodicity matches the binary's orbital period of 1.1 days, suggesting that the maser is triggered by the interaction between the two stars. This detection represents the first low-frequency observation of a flare star binary and the second instance of electron-cyclotron maser emission from a flare star, following the earlier discovery in UV Ceti. The findings imply that maser emission from these stars can persist for extended durations, potentially lasting days. Furthermore, the low-frequency nature of the emission suggests that future observations of maser activity in other flare star binaries may be feasible using LOFAR. These results also indicate that maser emission from flare stars can be detected at frequencies below 100 MHz, a range previously thought to be inaccessible. Finally, the data suggest that maser emission from flare stars may be detectable at frequencies lower than those of the Sun. These insights are crucial for understanding the physical mechanisms driving maser emission in flare stars and for planning future low-frequency radio surveys of the sky. Additionally, the study highlights the potential for using radio observations to investigate the magnetic fields of flare stars. We present findings from a cluster quantum Monte Carlo study of two-dimensional frustrated trimer antiferromagnets, specifically examining the triangular lattice of $S=1/2$ spins on triangles and the honeycomb lattice of $S=1/2$ spins on rhombi. Zero-shot learning (ZSL) enables models to classify unseen categories without additional training, a capability that is highly valuable for practical applications. While recent studies have demonstrated that pre-trained language models (PLMs) can achieve state-of-the-art results on image classification tasks using ZSL, they typically depend on extensive, manually crafted prompts. This paper introduces a novel approach to adapt PLMs for ZSL by meta-tuning them on a collection of prompts and datasets. Our method involves meta-tuning a PLM on a diverse set of prompts and datasets, followed by selecting the optimal prompt and model for a specific downstream task. We evaluate our approach on the ImageNet and COCO datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot image classification. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the learned prompt space, offering insights into the characteristics of effective prompts. We present a detailed analysis of the dynamical spin structure factor for the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice, utilizing both exact diagonalization and density matrix renormalization group methods. Our findings indicate that the system exhibits a rich spectrum of excitations, including a sharp magnon mode, a broad continuum, and a distinct low-energy mode. We demonstrate that the low-energy mode arises from the gapless nature of the 120-degree ordered ground state, whereas the continuum is attributed to the spin-liquid state found on the Kagome sublattice. Furthermore, we show that the low-energy mode can be interpreted as a manifestation of the spin-liquid state within the 120-degree ordered phase. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the phase diagram of the triangular lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet. This study introduces a kinetic model featuring a velocity-dependent collision frequency, designed to capture the effects of intermolecular potentials in rarefied gas flows. The model's collision frequency is derived from the inverse of the mean free path, which is calculated using the Lennard-Jones potential and the Boltzmann collision integral. The resulting kinetic equation is solved via the discrete velocity method, and its performance is evaluated against the constant collision frequency model and the Boltzmann equation. Numerical results indicate that the proposed model accurately reproduces the slip velocity and temperature jump at solid boundaries, as well as the Knudsen layer structure, across various Knudsen numbers. Furthermore, the model demonstrates excellent agreement with Boltzmann equation solutions for the same flow conditions. These findings suggest that the new kinetic model is highly effective for simulating rarefied gas flows. Finally, the model is applied to simulate the flow around a sphere, with results compared to those from the constant collision frequency model and the Boltzmann equation. The application confirms that the proposed model successfully reproduces the flow characteristics of a sphere under rarefied conditions. Overall, this work demonstrates that the new kinetic model can accurately simulate rarefied gas flows, offering a promising alternative to the Boltzmann equation. Additionally, the model's computational efficiency is significantly superior to that of the Boltzmann equation. Consequently, this new kinetic model is expected to be valuable for simulating rarefied gas flows in future research. The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is a proposed next-generation facility designed to investigate the internal structure of protons and nuclei by colliding them with high-energy electrons. To achieve the necessary high luminosity, the EIC will employ a 100 GeV electron beam and a 250 GeV proton or deuteron beam. The proposed silicon tracking detector will be positioned within a 1 Tesla solenoidal magnetic field, situated 10 cm from the interaction point. This device will feature a 10 cm radius vertex detector with 10 micrometer spatial resolution, a 10 cm radius central tracker offering 50 micrometer resolution, and an outer tracker with 100 micrometer resolution. The vertex detector will consist of 12 layers of silicon sensors, while the central and outer trackers will each comprise 16 layers. This paper outlines the sensor design and fabrication strategies for the vertex and central trackers, detailing the specific technologies selected for each component. Additionally, we present initial results from the first silicon sensor prototype, which was fabricated using a 150 micrometer thick epitaxial silicon layer. This prototype was successfully tested in a beamline at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. Finally, we discuss the sensor design and fabrication approach for the outer tracker. The proposed design utilizes a 300 micrometer thick epitaxial silicon layer, which is expected to provide sufficient charge collection for the outer tracker. We present spectropolarimetric observations of the A-type star HD58260, revealing a radial magnetic field slope of 1.2 kG across the stellar disk. This value aligns with the 1.3 kG slope previously inferred from the photometric modulation of the star's light curve. Furthermore, we estimated the magnetic field strength at the stellar equator to be 1.8 kG. These findings indicate that HD58260 possesses a strong, dipolar magnetic field, a characteristic shared with other chemically peculiar A-type stars. The observed magnetic field strength and slope are consistent with the star's evolutionary status as a pre-main-sequence object. Additionally, the magnetic field strength is comparable to that of the nearby A-type star HD168439, which is known to host a protoplanetary disk. This similarity suggests that HD58260 may also harbor a disk, a hypothesis supported by the detection of a 1.5 AU gap in its circumstellar environment. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the formation of planets around A-type stars. Our findings indicate that the H30$\alpha$ line is a reliable tracer of star formation, with a correlation coefficient of $r=0.92$ and a slope of $0.99 \pm 0.03$ when compared to H$\alpha$ luminosity. Furthermore, we compared H30$\alpha$ luminosity against other star formation indicators, including H$\alpha$ luminosity, the H$\alpha$/H$\beta$ ratio, and the H$\alpha$-derived star formation rate (SFR). The results show that H30$\alpha$ luminosity correlates well with H$\alpha$ luminosity ($r=0.92$) and the H$\alpha$/H$\beta$ ratio ($r=0.87$), but exhibits a weaker correlation with the H$\alpha$-derived SFR ($r=0.72$). Additionally, the H30$\alpha$-derived SFR demonstrates a strong correlation with H$\alpha$ luminosity ($r=0.92$) and the H$\alpha$/H$\beta$ ratio ($r=0.87$), while showing a weaker correlation with the H$\alpha$-derived SFR ($r=0.72$). These outcomes suggest that H30$\alpha$ luminosity is a robust star formation indicator, particularly in low-metallicity environments. Finally, we applied the H30$\alpha$-derived SFR to NGC 5253 to estimate the mass of the central compact object, yielding a value of $1.1 \times 10^6$ M$_{\odot}$. This mass aligns with the characteristics of an intermediate-mass black hole. Consequently, our study confirms that H30$\alpha$ luminosity serves as a reliable star formation tracer, especially for low-metallicity galaxies. The H30$\alpha$-derived SFR offers a valuable tool for estimating the mass of central compact objects in starburst galaxies. Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) are increasingly utilized to model real-world events, yet their dynamic nature introduces challenges for tasks like link prediction. This paper investigates the use of static models for link prediction within TKGs. We introduce a novel evaluation metric designed to assess static model performance on TKGs. Our findings indicate that static models can achieve state-of-the-art results on specific TKGs, particularly when employing a new loss function. Additionally, we demonstrate that static models can be effectively adapted for TKG link prediction by incorporating a new regularization technique. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the strengths and limitations of static models in this context. The code is accessible at https://github.com/robinvanlutterveld/StaticModelsTKG.

Keywords: Knowledge Graphs, Temporal Knowledge Graphs, Link Prediction, Static Models.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of the exponential equation $a^x=x$ for $a>0$, deriving asymptotic solutions for both $a>1$ and $0<a<1$. For the case $a>1$, we obtain a solution with an error term of $O(1/x)$, whereas for $0<a<1$, the error term is $O(1/x^2)$. Additionally, we provide a graphical representation of the solution when $a=e$. The study relies on the Lambert $W$ function, defined as the inverse of $f(x)=xe^x$. We present two distinct proofs for the $a>1$ case and a single proof for the $0<a<1$ case. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the solution in the $a>1$ scenario. Finally, we demonstrate that the solution to $a^x=x$ can be expressed as a power series in $1/x$ for both $a>1$ and $0<a<1$. The primary objective of this work is to offer a comprehensive analysis of the exponential equation $a^x=x$ for all $a>0$. We believe this study will be valuable to researchers and students in mathematics. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of the Lambert $W$ function, while Section 3 examines the asymptotic behavior of $a^x=x$ for $a>1$. Section 4 addresses the case $0<a<1$, and Section 5 presents a graphical solution for $a=e$. Section 6 explores the relationship between the solution and the Lambert $W$ function, and Section 7 concludes the study. We introduce a novel construction of high-dimensional extenders, which are fundamental combinatorial structures utilized in the design of pseudorandomness algorithms. Our approach relies on a specific type of cover known as a $(k, \ell)$-cover, defined as a collection of $k$-element subsets of an $n$-element set where every $\ell$-element subset is contained in at least one member of the collection. We demonstrate that for any $(k, \ell)$-cover $\mathcal{C}$, there exists a high-dimensional extender $\mathcal{E}$ such that $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{E}$. Furthermore, we establish that the size of $\mathcal{E}$ is bounded by $O(|\mathcal{C}| \cdot n^{\ell})$. This result yields a new upper bound for the size of high-dimensional extenders, improving upon the previous best bound of $O(n^{k})$. Additionally, we provide an explicit construction of these extenders. As a practical application, we utilize our extenders to construct a new class of pseudorandom generators, which are essential tools in derandomization. Finally, we present a lower bound for the size of extenders, demonstrating that our upper bound is nearly tight. The magnetic properties of the centered honeycomb antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$ were investigated using neutron diffraction and magnetization measurements. The data indicate that the Gd$^{3+}$ magnetic moments are arranged in a zigzag pattern within the $ab$-plane, with the moments in adjacent layers oriented antiparallel to one another. The magnetic structure is described by the propagation vector $\mathbf{k} = (1/2, 1/2, 1/2)$ and the magnetic unit cell parameters $a_m = 2a$ and $c_m = 4c$. The observed magnetic ordering temperature of 16.5 K aligns with the Curie temperature derived from magnetization data. Furthermore, the magnetic moment magnitude of 7.0 $\mu_B$ is consistent with the theoretical expectation for a Gd$^{3+}$ ion. The analysis of the magnetic structure reveals that the exchange interactions between nearest-neighbor Gd$^{3+}$ ions are ferromagnetic, whereas those between next-nearest-neighbor ions are antiferromagnetic. Additionally, the magnetic anisotropy is determined to be uniaxial along the $c$-axis. Finally, the magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$ are compared with those of other honeycomb antiferromagnets. These findings suggest that the magnetic characteristics of GdInO$_3$ are primarily governed by the exchange interactions between next-nearest-neighbor Gd$^{3+}$ ions. Consequently, GdInO$_3$ is classified as a quasi two-dimensional centered honeycomb antiferromagnet. The study concludes by discussing the implications of these results for the electronic structure of GdInO$_3$. This paper introduces a novel deep learning approach for integrating infrared and visible imagery to detect wildfires. The method utilizes a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to create a new infrared channel that combines the thermal data from the infrared sensor with the spatial details of the visible sensor. This synthetic channel is then fused with the original infrared and visible images to generate a composite image optimized for wildfire detection. The proposed technique is evaluated using the FireVid dataset, which comprises 1,000 image triplets (infrared, visible, and integrated) from 100 wildfires. Experimental results demonstrate that the generated images are highly suitable for detection tasks, achieving a 10% improvement in the F1-score compared to using the original infrared images alone. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against variations in the number of wildfires and the count of visible images used for training. This study introduces a stochastic compartmental model for COVID-19, where each compartment is defined as a random variable representing the count of individuals in a specific state. The model's dynamics are governed by a system of stochastic differential equations. We derive the corresponding deterministic mean-field model and establish the existence and uniqueness of its solution. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of the disease-free equilibrium and provide numerical simulations to validate our theoretical findings. Finally, we calculate the basic reproduction number for COVID-19 within this framework. The results indicate that the disease-free equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable when the basic reproduction number is less than one, and unstable when it exceeds one. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model admits a unique global positive solution. The paper concludes with a discussion of these findings. The isoscalar giant monopole resonance (ISGMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si was investigated using the quasiparticle random phase approximation (QRPA) with a Skyrme interaction, incorporating coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole excitations. This coupling was modeled by including the quadrupole component of the monopole operator within the QRPA framework. The resulting ISGMR energies and widths for both nuclei were compared against experimental data. The analysis indicates that the coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole excitations significantly influences the ISGMR strength distribution, particularly in $^{24}$Mg. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the monopole and quadrupole components of the isoscalar monopole operator are essential for accurately reproducing the ISGMR strength distribution in $^{24}$Mg. We introduce a deep reinforcement learning approach designed to optimize the dynamic reinsurance treaty for an insurer. The insurer's objective is to maximize the expected discounted utility of its terminal wealth, with the reinsurance treaty serving as the control variable. This control is modeled as a stochastic process that evolves over time based on the insurer's current state. We demonstrate that the optimal reinsurance strategy can be characterized by a Hamilton-Jacobi-Quasi-Variational-Inequality (HJQVI) and propose a deep reinforcement learning algorithm to solve it. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the method's effectiveness. Furthermore, we examine the impact of various model parameters on the optimal reinsurance strategy. Finally, we compare our findings with those from a static reinsurance framework. The results indicate that a dynamic reinsurance strategy can yield higher expected utility for the insurer compared to a static one. Additionally, the optimal dynamic strategy is shown to be highly sensitive to the insurer's risk aversion and the correlation between the insurer's and reinsurer's asset returns. In contrast, the optimal static strategy is less sensitive to these factors. These insights are valuable for both insurers and reinsurers when designing and pricing reinsurance products. Sequential recommender systems are essential for delivering personalized suggestions in e-commerce and content streaming. However, current state-of-the-art models often fail to capture the underlying intent of users, leading to irrelevant recommendations. To address this, we introduce a new approach that explicitly models user intent by learning a latent purpose representation from user-item interactions. This method is integrated into a sequential recommender framework to generate personalized item sequences. We evaluated our model on two real-world datasets, Amazon and Spotify, and compared it against state-of-the-art baselines. The results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in both recommendation accuracy and diversity. Furthermore, we show that the learned latent purpose representations can be effectively utilized for downstream tasks, such as clustering users with similar intents. The source code is available at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1997/LUP.

This study examines the estimation of a rank-one matrix under groupwise heteroskedasticity, where the noise covariance matrix is block-diagonal. We establish minimax lower bounds for the risk associated with estimating the underlying signal matrix. Our analysis reveals that the minimax risk is governed by the harmonic mean of the signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) across all groups. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the minimax rate for this problem is identical to that of a homoskedastic setting, provided the SNR is defined as the harmonic mean of group-specific SNRs. We also derive a minimax upper bound for a specific estimator, showing that its risk converges to the minimax risk as the number of groups increases. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations. These results are applicable to various statistical challenges, including matrix completion, denoising, and principal component analysis. Additionally, we illustrate the relevance of this work to the analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/MatrixEstimation. We introduce a topological model that lacks symmetry protection and is defined by a non-trivial Chern number. This model is derived from a tight-binding framework featuring a single orbital per unit cell, where the energy dispersion is determined by the ratio of two hopping amplitudes. The resulting band structure exhibits two Dirac points, which are separated by a finite energy gap. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics of this model can be tuned by adjusting the phase of the second hopping amplitude. Finally, we validate the topological nature of this model through numerical simulations of the quantum Hall effect. These findings suggest that the proposed model could be realized in various physical systems, including cold atoms, photonic crystals, and electronic systems. Additionally, we show that the model can be extended to a two-orbital system, which supports a non-trivial $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant. This extension is also applicable to cold atom, photonic crystal, and electronic systems. Consequently, the model offers a promising avenue for investigating topological phenomena in diverse physical contexts. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant global disruption, with the World Health Organization reporting over 100 million confirmed cases and more than 2 million deaths. While numerous studies have examined the disease's spread, the impact of social media on its transmission remains underexplored. The first stage employs a BERT-based model to classify tweets as either COVID-19 related or not, while the second stage utilizes a BERT-based model to further sub-categorize the identified tweets. Additionally, the research highlights the critical role of social media in the dissemination of COVID-19 information. Eco-evolutionary dynamics (EED) describe the reciprocal interactions between ecological and evolutionary processes. While these processes are often viewed as distinct, they frequently occur simultaneously, with their relative speeds determined by the timescales of ecological and evolutionary change. This review examines the factors influencing these timescales and the rate modulators that drive them. We explore how these elements interact to shape the temporal dynamics of EED, emphasizing the critical role of timescale mismatches. Furthermore, we analyze how these dynamics alter the stability of ecological and evolutionary equilibria, the nature of coexistence, and the maintenance of biodiversity. Finally, we outline the implications of these findings for understanding the origins of biodiversity and the mechanisms of adaptation. The review concludes by identifying key areas for future research. Sensitivity analysis is essential for drawing valid conclusions from incomplete datasets. This study introduces a Bayesian framework for sensitivity analysis that integrates a prior distribution for the missing data mechanism with an E-value to quantify the robustness of findings against untestable assumptions. The E-value represents the ratio of the posterior probability of a specific parameter value to its prior probability, thereby measuring the degree of learning achieved. We demonstrate the application of this approach through a simulation study and a real-world analysis of the 2016 US Presidential Election. The results indicate that the proposed method effectively evaluates the robustness of inferences derived from missing data. Furthermore, the method is straightforward to implement and can be readily adapted to various contexts. Consequently, this approach offers a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners to assess the reliability of their findings when dealing with missing data.
